title: Uniform Resource Locators (URL)
summary: Specifies the Uniform Resource Locator (URL), the syntax and semantics of formalized strings that name the location and access method for resources on the Internet. It is on the standards track. It has been replaced by later documents, including RFC 4248 and RFC 4266.

plainLanguage.summary: A URL is a text form that names an Internet resource and tells a program how to access it. This RFC defines a shared structure and describes several scheme-specific forms.

questions: what characters must be encoded in a url
what are the default ports for url schemes
subtitle: The 1994 definition of URLs: strings that identify a resource and describe how to access it.

tldr.problem: Internet resources could be accessed through different protocols, but people needed a compact and consistent way to write their locations.
tldr.mechanism: A URL combines a scheme with scheme-specific information. The RFC defines common syntax and describes schemes for services such as FTP, HTTP, mail, and news.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1738 is obsoleted by RFC 4248 and RFC 4266 and has been updated by later RFCs, according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 1738 is obsoleted by RFC 4248 and RFC 4266. The unit metadata also lists several later updates, including RFC 3986.

sections.title: The Basic URL Structure
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is a compact string for locating a resource available through the Internet. It starts with a scheme name, then a colon, then information whose meaning depends on that scheme.

Scheme names may contain lowercase letters, digits, plus signs, periods, and hyphens. Programs interpreting a URL should treat uppercase and lowercase scheme letters as equivalent. The scheme indicates the access method, while the rest identifies the resource according to that method.
sections.plainLanguage: A URL starts with a scheme name and a colon. The remaining text gives details that the named access method understands.

sections.title: Characters and Percent Encoding
sections.content:
URLs use printable US-ASCII characters. An octet that cannot be written as a graphic US-ASCII character, is unsafe, or is reserved for a scheme must be encoded as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits.

The RFC lists spaces, angle brackets, quotation marks, number signs, percent signs, and other characters that must be encoded because they may be changed or interpreted specially. Characters such as slash, question mark, colon, at sign, equals sign, and ampersand may be reserved by a scheme, so their encoded form can have a different meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters can break or change a URL. The RFC writes those characters as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits.

sections.title: The Shared Host-Based Form
sections.content:
Many schemes that use an IP-based protocol to contact a host share a structure with optional user name, password, host, port, and path fields. The scheme-specific part begins with two slashes. The host can be a fully qualified domain name or an IPv4 address.

The port is written in decimal and may be omitted when the scheme has a default. The path is interpreted according to the scheme. Some schemes use slashes to separate hierarchical parts, but this RFC does not define relative links.
sections.plainLanguage: Many URLs identify a host and may also include a port and path. The scheme determines how a program interprets those parts.

sections.title: The Schemes Defined in the RFC
sections.content:
RFC 1738 describes ten schemes: ftp, http, gopher, mailto, news, nntp, telnet, wais, file, and prospero. They identify different kinds of resources or services. For example, an HTTP URL identifies a resource accessed with HTTP, while a mailto URL identifies a mailing address.

Some schemes identify a specific host and resource path. Others, such as news, can identify a group or message without naming one server. A file URL names a file on a host, or on the local machine when its host is empty or localhost.
sections.plainLanguage: Each scheme has rules for a particular service or kind of resource. A URL's scheme tells a program which rules to apply.

sections.title: Registering Schemes and Handling URLs Safely
sections.content:
The RFC says new schemes need a defined access algorithm and syntax, and should demonstrate usefulness and operability. IANA maintains a registry of URL schemes. Names beginning with x- are reserved for experimental use.

A URL does not guarantee that it will continue to identify the same object. A non-default port can make a client contact a service using an unexpected protocol, and encoded delimiters must not be decoded before transmission if that would change protocol commands. The RFC warns against putting secret passwords in URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: New schemes need defined rules and registration. A URL can also cause an unexpected operation if a program sends it to the wrong service, so secret passwords should not be included.
